implementation_notes: Model-first: the struct is the contract, serde attributes (#[serde(rename, default, deny_unknown_fields)]) decide wire names and tolerance, serde_json::to_string/from_str own the wire form, and #[derive(JsonSchema)] with schema_for!() emits the JSON Schema document that is published to consumers - the codec and the artifact cannot drift because both come from the same types. Choose the schema-first variant (prost) when the schema must generate bindings into several languages. The generated-binding-plus-translator structure is still justified when the published shape differs from the domain types: keep a wire module with its own types and an explicit conversion.
pitfalls: deny_unknown_fields is a decision, not a default: it rejects producer additions while plain serde ignores unknown keys - make the tolerance policy explicit in the published language.
serde_json refuses integers outside i64/u64 and offers no lossless JSON number type: ids and money must travel as fixed-width integers, strings or a decimal type.
A struct field rename without #[serde(rename)] silently changes the published property name; publish the derived schema in CI and diff it so the change is visible.

variants.name: Protocol Buffers with prost-generated types
variants.implementation_notes: Schema-first: the .proto file is the published language, prost-build in build.rs emits Rust structs implementing prost::Message, and encode_to_vec()/decode() speak the documented binary form while the same artifact generates bindings for every other participant. Pick it when the contract is polyglot and evolution has to be governed by field numbers; pick the serde/schemars default when the JSON document is the language and the Rust types are the source of truth. Unknown fields are preserved on decode, which keeps old binaries readable against new producers.
pitfalls: prost does not generate the .proto itself: the schema lives outside the crate and must be released together with the generated code, or producer and consumer compile against different contracts.
decode() failures include both malformed wire data and schema skew; route them to the invalid-message path and never unwrap inside a handler.
prost types are plain structs with public fields, so domain code can start using wire types directly - keep the generated module private and convert at the seam.
